common_name: Masai Bush Bean (French Filet Bush Bean, AAS Winner)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to 60°F; Masai is a compact bush-type filet bean that stays productive over a longer window than most bush filet types before needing succession sowing.

directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 3-4 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest every 1-2 days once pods reach 4-5 inches and are still pencil-thin. Masai is an American Award of Merit-winning French filet bush bean, prized for combining the slender, tender, seedless-tasting pods typical of haricots verts with a compact, upright, easy-to-harvest bush habit that needs no trellising. The plants hold their pods up off the ground and above the foliage, making picking fast and keeping pods cleaner and less prone to soil-splash disease than sprawling bush types. Because filet beans mature quickly from flower to overgrown pod, harvest frequently to maintain the fine, tender texture; pods left even a day or two too long become coarser and more fibrous. Succession sow every 2-3 weeks through the season for a continuous harvest, since bush types produce a concentrated flush rather than the extended season of pole filet beans.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Filet Bean Growing Guide

common_name: Lutz Green Leaf Beet (Winter Keeper Storage Beet)

planting.note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9; Lutz is a late-maturing beet bred specifically for long storage rather than early eating, so allow it a full season to size up.

directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3-4 inches once true leaves appear; keep soil consistently moist to prevent woody roots. Lutz Green Leaf, also called Winter Keeper, is a classic American heirloom beet bred to grow to a large size (often 3-5 inches or more) without becoming woody, fibrous, or losing its sweet flavor the way most beets do when oversized — a trait that makes it uniquely suited for fall harvest and long winter root-cellar storage. The tender, mild, sweet flesh holds its quality even at full size, and the abundant deep green tops are excellent cooked as beet greens. Because it needs a longer season to develop its full storage-quality size, plant it in time to mature before hard frost, then harvest and store roots in damp sand or a root cellar for use well into winter.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Lutz Green Leaf variety notes

planting.note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9; succession sow through the cool season for a continuous harvest.

directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3-4 inches once true leaves appear; keep soil consistently moist for smooth, tender roots. Forono is an Italian heirloom beet distinguished by its long, cylindrical, carrot-like shape rather than the typical round beet form, an advantage in the kitchen because its uniform diameter yields evenly sized slices from end to end with almost no waste, and a single root often provides several servings. The deep red flesh is sweet, tender, and free of the pale internal rings some other beets show, and because the roots grow mostly upward out of the soil rather than swelling wide, more roots can be grown in the same row space. Harvest at 4-6 inches long for the best texture, and the tops are also good cooked as greens.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Forono variety notes

common_name: Moulin Rouge Beet (Uniform Cylindrical Hybrid Beet)

planting.note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9; succession sow through the cool season for a continuous harvest.

directions: Sow half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3-4 inches once true leaves appear; keep soil consistently moist for smooth, evenly shaped roots. Moulin Rouge is a modern hybrid cylindrical beet, similar in form to heirloom cylindrical types like Forono but bred for more uniform root shape, smoother skin, and reliable germination and sizing, making slicing and pickling more efficient with less trimming waste. The deep red, sweet, tender flesh holds its color well when cooked, and the long, straight roots make it a favorite for home canning and pickling where consistent slice size matters. Because the roots grow mostly upright rather than wide, plants can be spaced somewhat closer than round beet varieties for the same yield. The greens are also edible and good cooked as beet greens.
sources: Renee's Garden Seeds — Moulin Rouge variety notes
